properties.notes: A stop on the Lech at Fussen, where the road came down off the mountains into the province of Raetia proper before the last stretch to Augusta Vindelicum.

properties.name: Augusta Vindelicum
properties.notes: Augsburg today, and the road's real destination -- the provincial capital of Raetia that Drusus and Claudius spent sixty years of road-building trying to connect to the Adriatic. Not yet on this map as a full city; the road stops here for now.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Augsburger Siegesaltar, eradierte Stelle mit Nennung des Konsuls Honoratianus.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Augsburger Siegesaltar / Römisches Museum Augsburg
properties.image_alt: Detail of the Augsburg Victory Altar (dedicated 260 CE, found 1992), the Roman altar to Victoria commemorating the defeat of the Juthungi near Augusta Vindelicum, now in the Römisches Museum Augsburg

properties.name: Submuntorium
properties.notes: A fort and river-post on the upper Danube where a spur of the road reached the frontier, roughly 30km north of Augsburg. Some scholars place the name at nearby Neuburg instead of Burghofe -- the site is secure, the exact ancient label less so.

properties.name: Ponte Mammolo
properties.notes: A bridge over the Aniene just outside Rome's walls, the first landmark on the road out to Tibur. The modern bridge on the same site still carries the road's descendant highway.
properties.image_credit: Ponte Mammolo, engraving by Giuseppe Vasi, 18th century · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 18th-century Giuseppe Vasi engraving of Ponte Mammolo, the Roman-era bridge carrying the Via Tiburtina over the Aniene.

properties.name: Aquae Albulae
properties.notes: A statio at the sulfur springs six kilometers short of Tibur, their milky-blue water so strong-smelling that Pliny, Strabo and Isidore all singled it out. Romans travelled out from the city just to bathe here, the way people still do today at the same springs.
properties.image_credit: Aquae Albulae thermal springs, Bagni di Tivoli · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Lago della Regina, one of the sulphurous Aquae Albulae springs near Tivoli on the Via Tiburtina

properties.name: Vicovaro
properties.notes: Vicus Varia sat where the road left the Aniene valley for the climb toward the Aequian hills, at the point the Via Sublacensis split off toward Subiaco. Its name survives almost unchanged in the modern town.

properties.name: Carseoli
properties.notes: A Latin colony planted in Aequian territory in 298 BCE, well before the road that would later run through it. By 117 CE it was a working stop on the climb toward the Fucine Lake basin.

properties.name: Alba Fucens
properties.notes: A frontier colony planted in 303 BCE between the Marsi and the Aequi, high on the shoulder of Monte Velino above the Fucine Lake. Rome kept its most dangerous prisoners here -- Syphax of Numidia died in custody at Alba Fucens, and King Perseus of Macedon, the last man to rule as a Hellenistic king, ended his life here too.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre at Alba Fucens · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Amphitheatre ruins at Alba Fucens

properties.name: Marruvium
properties.notes: The chief town of the Marsi, on the eastern shore of the Fucine Lake -- a people Rome fought hard against in the Social War and then leaned on hard for legionaries afterward. The lake itself, since drained, made the town a lakeside stop rather than the landlocked ruin it is today.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre at Marruvium, San Benedetto dei Marsi · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Amphitheatre ruins of Marruvium

properties.name: Corfinio
properties.notes: The Italian rebels of the Social War made Corfinium their capital in 91 BCE and renamed it Italica -- a rival Rome built to hold its own name and its own senate. It lost that war and went back to being an ordinary Roman town, but the memory of the challenge stuck to the place for a long time after.

properties.name: Interpromium
properties.notes: A relay station in the Aternus valley below modern San Valentino in Abruzzo Citeriore. The Itineraries give it as 12 Roman miles from Corfinium, but that figure doesn't square with the geodesic distance between the two identified sites closely enough to trust on this ground-coordinate precision, so it ships unclaimed here rather than forced.

properties.name: Chieti
properties.notes: Teate, chief town of the Marrucini, sat on a hill above the Aternus valley -- a defensible perch that is why modern Chieti still looks down on the Pescara plain from the same spot.

properties.name: Pescara
properties.notes: The road's Adriatic terminus, where the Aternus river reaches the sea -- 9 Roman miles past Teate by the Itineraries' own count, and 21 from Interpromium, both figures the ground still bears out. A modest port town in 117 CE, nothing like the city that grew from it.

properties.name: Nola
properties.notes: The first major stop south of Capua on the road to Rhegium, and later the town where Augustus died on 19 August 14 CE. A specific Antonine Itinerary mileage for this leg turned up in only one unreliable source, so no distance figure is claimed here.
sources: Itinerarium Antonini, Regium-Capuam route (loose citation, exact section unconfirmed)

properties.name: Nuceria Alfaterna
properties.notes: Modern Nocera Superiore/Inferiore. The Republican-era Lapis Pollae milestone (CIL I2 638), found at Forum Popilii, gives 51 Roman miles from there to Nuceria — the strongest single piece of evidence placing this town squarely on the Via Popilia mainline.
properties.image_credit: Hellenistic-Roman theatre of Nuceria Alfaterna, Nocera Superiore · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ancient theatre at Nuceria Alfaterna

properties.name: Salernum
properties.notes: Modern Salerno. A Latin colony planted in 194 BCE on the Gulf of Salerno, partly to hold the coast after the Picentini were resettled inland — it sat directly on the road south toward the Vallo di Diano.

properties.name: Picentia
properties.notes: Modern Pontecagnano Faiano. Resettled with Picentes displaced from the Adriatic coast in 268 BCE; whether it sat on the Via Popilia's mainline or a coastal spur is not fully settled in the sources found.
sources: Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites, s.v. Picentia (via search)
properties.image_credit: Archaeological remains of Picentia, Pontecagnano Faiano · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins at the site of ancient Picentia

properties.name: Eburum
properties.notes: Modern Eboli, the gateway from the Sele coastal plain into the Vallo di Diano interior that the road follows south.

properties.name: Acerronia
properties.notes: Near modern Auletta, a waystation on the Vallo di Diano stretch of the road between Eburum and the Nares Lucanae narrows.

properties.name: Nares Lucanae
properties.notes: "The Narrows of Lucania," a mountain passage near Sicignano degli Alburni whose exact location is disputed between three nearby candidate sites — shipped here as the interpolated corridor midpoint rather than a specific excavated spot.

properties.name: Atina
properties.notes: Modern Atena Lucana, one of a tight cluster of stations serving the Vallo di Diano valley floor.

properties.name: Consilinum
properties.notes: Modern Sala Consilina preserves the Roman name almost unchanged, one of the more securely identified stops in the Vallo di Diano.

properties.name: Marcellianum
properties.notes: A roadside settlement at San Giovanni in Fonte, later home to a paleochristian baptistery Cassiodorus is recorded visiting in the early 6th century.
sources: Comune di Sala Consilina, local history pages (via search)
properties.image_credit: Later mosaic (c. 390 CE) at the baptistery on the site of Marcellianum, near Sala Consilina · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Late-antique mosaic at the site of Marcellianum, centuries after this map's 117 CE snapshot

properties.name: Tegianum
properties.notes: Modern Teggiano, another Vallo di Diano stop on the road south toward the Lucanian mountains.

properties.name: Forum Popilii
properties.notes: Modern Polla — the town literally named for the consul who built this road, Publius Popillius Laenas. Site of the Lapis Pollae milestone (CIL I2 638), a Republican-era inscription recording cumulative distances from here to Nuceria, Capua, Muranum, Cosentia, Valentia and Regium — the single best source for the road's overall shape.
properties.image_credit: The Lapis Pollae (Elogium of Polla), Roman inscription recording the Via Popilia route, found at Polla (Forum Popilii) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Latin inscription describing the Via Popilia, found at Polla

properties.name: Nerulum
properties.notes: An ancient Lucanian town taken by Rome in 317 BCE (Livy). Modern identification is contested between Rotonda and Lagonegro; the Barrington Atlas favors Rotonda, used here.

properties.name: Muranum
properties.notes: Modern Morano Calabro. Fixed both by the Antonine Itinerary (14 Roman miles from Nerulum) and independently by the Lapis Pollae (74 miles from Forum Popilii) — a rare case where two ancient sources agree.

properties.name: Caprasia
properties.notes: Near modern Castrovillari (contrada Ciparsia, which preserves the name). Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography places it on this stretch, roughly 28 miles from Consentia, though its exact position relative to the next station wasn't confirmable enough to attach that figure here.
sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography, s.v. Consentia (via search)

properties.name: Interamnium
properties.notes: Modern San Lorenzo del Vallo — the name means "between two rivers," describing its position between the Crati's tributaries on the way down to Consentia.
sources: Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire (DARE), imperium.ahlfeldt.se/places/22548.html

properties.name: Consentia
properties.notes: Modern Cosenza, capital of the Bruttii — the Lapis Pollae places it 123 Roman miles from Forum Popilii, a major waypoint on the road's long southern leg.

properties.name: Ad Fluvium Sabatum
properties.notes: A river-crossing station where the road forded the Savuto, in the Savuto-Reventino area. The exact ford location is still debated in the modern archaeological literature and has never been pinned to one excavated spot.
sources: Roberto Spadea et al., "La via Regio-Capuam nell'area del Savuto-Reventino," academia.edu/39901904

properties.name: Ad Turres
properties.notes: Modern Sambiase, now part of Lamezia Terme, named for a pair of Roman watchtowers that once stood here. The station also appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana.

properties.name: Vibo Valentia
properties.notes: A Latin colony founded in 192 BCE on the site of the Greek city of Hipponion. The Antonine Itinerary's mileage from Ad Turres to here does not clear a straight-line sanity check against these two towns' real coordinates, so no figure is claimed for this leg.
properties.image_credit: State Archaeological Museum at Vibo Valentia, ancient Vibo Valentia/Hipponion · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Archaeological museum building at Vibo Valentia

properties.name: Nicotera
properties.notes: One of the few stations on this road to keep its ancient name essentially unchanged into the modern town.

properties.name: Ad Mallias
properties.notes: Modern Bagnara Calabra, on the coast road running down toward the Strait of Messina crossing.

properties.name: Columna
properties.notes: "Columna Rhegia," a marker station near modern Cannitello at the narrowest ferry crossing to Sicily — the site was never definitively excavated, so several nearby candidate points have been proposed.
sources: Local Calabrian antiquarian sources (via search); site position approximate

properties.name: Regium
properties.notes: Modern Reggio Calabria, the road's terminus at the Strait of Messina — the closest crossing point to Sicily and the end of a road that ran the full length of the Italian peninsula's toe.
properties.image_credit: Mosaic floor of the Roman baths (Terme Romane) of Regium, Reggio Calabria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Mosaic floor of the Roman baths at Reggio Calabria

properties.name: Gabii
properties.notes: An old Latin League city 12 Roman miles from Rome — the road out to it was originally called Via Gabina before its later extension to Praeneste gave the whole route its familiar name.
properties.image_credit: Bronze portrait bust found at Gabii, now in the Louvre · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman bronze bust excavated at Gabii

properties.name: Ad Quintanas
properties.notes: Took its name from colonists of Labicum settled on land divided into quintana plots, per Livy. Location approximate along the known route rather than a pinned excavated point.

properties.name: Ad Statuas
properties.notes: Near modern San Cesareo, named for a profusion of decorative statuary and the point where the road forked toward Tusculum, Praeneste and Gabii. A cistern faced in Severan-era brickwork survives nearby. The Itinerary's claimed 3 mp from Ad Quintanas doesn't clear a straight-line sanity check against these two sites' real coordinates, so no distance figure is claimed for this leg.
sources: Nibby, Analisi storico-topografica-antiquaria della carta de' dintorni di Roma

properties.name: Ad Pictas
properties.notes: Located near Valle Fredda in Valmontone's territory by a 2013 scholarly study identifying the Via Labicana's route through this stretch.
sources: "The Via Latina, the Via Labicana and the location of Ad Pictas," Papers of the British School at Rome (2013)

properties.name: Ad Bivium
properties.notes: "At the fork" — the Tabula Peutingeriana's largest Via Labicana station, 30 Roman miles from Rome, where the road split toward the Via Latina. The catacomb of Sant'Ilario was excavated on the same site.
sources: Rivista di Archeologia Cristiana 99 (2023), on the Ad Bivium excavation

properties.name: Ficulea
properties.notes: An old Latin League town that gave the road its original name, Via Ficulensis, before it was extended to Nomentum. Its precise site remains debated among 19th-century and modern topographers alike; no Roman-mile figure for the distance from Rome could be sourced with confidence.

properties.name: Compitum Anagninum
properties.notes: Excavated 2007-08 at Osteria della Fontana below Anagni, revealing a Temple of Diana and a structure nicknamed the "Circo Marittimo" beside a since-vanished sacred lake. The point where the Via Latina, Via Labicana and the Praenestina's extension physically converge in the Sacco valley.
sources: anagnia.com, Osteria della Fontana excavation reports

properties.name: Ferentinum
properties.notes: Modern Ferentino, a Hernician hill town on the Via Latina's climb through the Sacco valley.
properties.image_credit: Acropolis of Ferentino (ancient Ferentinum) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Path climbing toward the ancient acropolis of Ferentino, the Roman Ferentinum on the Via Latina.

properties.name: Frusino
properties.notes: Modern Frosinone, another Hernician town absorbed early into Rome's road network.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre of Frosinone (ancient Frusino) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman amphitheatre remains, Frosinone

properties.name: Fregellanum
properties.notes: Fregellae, a major Latin colony founded in 328 BCE, was destroyed by Rome in 125 BCE after leading a revolt. Its road station lived on afterward under the diminished name Fregellanum, across the Liri from its replacement colony, Fabrateria Nova.
properties.image_credit: Roman baths at Fregellae · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Excavated remains of the Roman baths at Fregellae, the destroyed Latin colony on the Via Latina.

properties.name: Fabrateria Nova
properties.notes: Founded to resettle Fregellae's survivors after Rome razed their city in 125 BCE, sited just across the Liri river from the ruins. Distinct from the older, separate town of Fabrateria Vetus near modern Ceccano, off this stretch of road.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Ritratto di livia, 58 ac., 29 dc, da san giovanni incarico.JPG?width=800
properties.image_credit: Portrait of Livia found at San Giovanni Incarico, site of Fabrateria Nova · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman marble portrait of Livia excavated at San Giovanni Incarico, the site of ancient Fabrateria Nova.

properties.name: Aquinum
properties.notes: Modern Aquino, birthplace of the satirist Juvenal, with a substantial surviving amphitheater and forum. The Itinerary's claimed 8 mp from Fabrateria Nova doesn't clear a straight-line sanity check against these two towns' real coordinates, so no distance figure is claimed for this leg.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Mark Antony, Aquino, ancient Aquinum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Roman triumphal Arch of Mark Antony still standing in Aquino, ancient Aquinum on the Via Latina.

properties.name: Casinum
properties.notes: Modern Cassino. Ummidia Quadratilla, a wealthy local benefactor, funded the town's surviving amphitheater and theater.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre of Casinum, Cassino · Wikimedia Commons (reused, same site as politics_senator_casinum)

properties.name: Venafrum
properties.notes: Modern Venafro, renowned in antiquity for the quality of its olive oil — Cato and Varro both praised Venafran oil as the best in Italy.

properties.name: Teanum Sidicinum
properties.notes: Modern Teano, capital of the Sidicini before Rome absorbed the town — a major road junction where this Beneventum-bound branch of the Via Latina met the route continuing on to Casilinum and the Via Appia near Capua.
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre of Teano (ancient Teanum Sidicinum) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman theatre ruins at Teano

properties.name: Alifae
properties.notes: Modern Alife, an old Samnite town on the road's final stretch toward Beneventum.
properties.image_credit: Entrance to the Roman cryptoporticus at Alife (ancient Alifae) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman underground gallery at Alife

properties.name: Telesia
properties.notes: Near modern San Salvatore Telesino, the last stop before Beneventum on this branch of the Via Latina.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre at Telesia, near San Salvatore Telesino · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Amphitheatre ruins at Telesia

properties.name: Rutupiae
properties.notes: The main Roman gateway into Britain — modern Richborough, Kent. Founded as the beachhead for the 43 CE invasion, it grew into a fortified supply port with its own monumental arch, and every legion, official and letter crossing the Channel to the province passed through here.
properties.image_credit: Richborough Roman Fort (Rutupiae), Kent · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Roman fort at Richborough

properties.name: Durovernum Cantiacorum
properties.notes: Modern Canterbury, Kent — a civitas capital of the Cantiaci on the direct road between Londinium and the Channel port at Rutupiae. Excavations have found a Roman theatre and public baths beneath the later medieval city.
properties.image_credit: Surviving section of Canterbury's city wall, on the line of the Roman circuit of Durovernum Cantiacorum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Old city wall in Canterbury

properties.name: Durolevum
properties.notes: A staging post the Antonine Itinerary places between Durobrivae and Durovernum, but archaeologists still disagree on its exact site — candidates cluster around Ospringe and Syndale near modern Faversham.

properties.name: Durobrivae
properties.notes: Modern Rochester, Kent, where Watling Street crossed the tidal River Medway. A bridge here carried the road since at least the 1st century CE, and the crossing gave the town its name — durobrivae means roughly 'fort by the bridges.'

properties.name: Sulloniacis
properties.notes: A staging post at Brockley Hill, Stanmore, on the ridge northwest of Londinium — excavation has turned up large-scale pottery kilns here supplying the capital with tableware.

properties.name: Verulamium
properties.notes: Modern St Albans, one of only three Romano-British towns granted the high status of municipium. It was sacked and burned during Boudica's revolt in 60/61 CE, then rebuilt with a forum, basilica and theatre — thriving again well before Trajan's reign.
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre of Verulamium, St Albans · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman theatre at Verulamium

properties.name: Durocobrivis
properties.notes: A mansio at modern Dunstable, Bedfordshire, where Watling Street crosses the prehistoric Icknield Way — a road junction of real strategic value, not just a rest stop.

properties.name: Magiovinium
properties.notes: A walled way-station near modern Fenny Stratford, Milton Keynes, where excavation has recovered a defended enclosure alongside the road plus a scatter of Roman-period burials in the surrounding fields.

properties.name: Lactodurum
properties.notes: Modern Towcester, Northamptonshire — a defended small town that grew up around its Watling Street mansio, with a ditched enclosure still traceable in the town's later medieval street plan.

properties.name: Bannaventa
properties.notes: A roadside settlement at Whilton Lodge, Northamptonshire, that grew into a proper small town with its own defenses by the later Roman period — one of several Watling Street vici that outgrew their original function as a simple stopping point.

properties.name: Tripontium
properties.notes: A mansio at Cave's Inn, Shawell, Warwickshire, named for the three bridges that once carried the road over the River Avon and its side channels here.

properties.name: Venonis
properties.notes: The junction at High Cross, Leicestershire, where Watling Street crosses the Fosse Way — the two great cross-country roads of Roman Britain meeting at a single point, making this one of the busiest crossroads in the province.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/High Cross Watling Street - Fosse Way - geograph.org.uk - 863077.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: The modern monument marking the Watling Street / Fosse Way crossing at Venonis, High Cross — not a Roman-period structure itself · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: High Cross monument at the Roman road junction

properties.name: Manduessedum
properties.notes: Modern Mancetter, Warwickshire — a mansio and small fort site, traditionally linked by local tradition (though not firmly proven) to the general area of Boudica's last battle against Rome in 60/61 CE.

properties.name: Letocetum
properties.notes: Modern Wall, Staffordshire — one of the best-excavated mansiones in Britain, with a substantial bathhouse and guest inn still standing to window height, run for travelers and imperial couriers on the road.
properties.image_credit: Remains of the Letocetum Roman bathhouse, Wall, Staffordshire · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman bathhouse foundations at Letocetum

properties.name: Pennocrucium
properties.notes: A mansio at Water Eaton, Staffordshire, where Watling Street crossed a tributary of the River Penk — the name itself is Brittonic for roughly 'chief crossing.'

properties.name: Uxacona
properties.notes: A roadside settlement at Redhill, Shropshire, on the final stretch of Watling Street before it reached Viroconium — one of the lesser-excavated stations on this road, known mainly from itinerary sources.

properties.name: Viroconium Cornoviorum
properties.notes: Modern Wroxeter, Shropshire — Watling Street's northwestern terminus and, by the early 2nd century, the fourth-largest city in Roman Britain, civitas capital of the Cornovii with a monumental forum and one of the largest known Roman bathhouses in the province.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Viroconium Cornoviorum, Wroxeter · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Standing Roman masonry at Wroxeter

properties.name: Isca Dumnoniorum
properties.notes: Modern Exeter, Devon — the Fosse Way's southwestern terminus and civitas capital of the Dumnonii, built over an earlier legionary fortress once garrisoned by Legio II Augusta.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Exeter city wall near the cathedral - geograph.org.uk - 266554.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Section of Exeter's city wall, built on the Roman circuit of Isca Dumnoniorum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Old stone wall near Exeter Cathedral

properties.name: Lindinis
properties.notes: Modern Ilchester, Somerset — a mansio that later grew important enough to become the seat of its own civitas, the Durotriges Lendinienses, splitting administrative duties with Dorchester.

properties.name: Aquae Sulis
properties.notes: Modern Bath, Somerset, where the Fosse Way met a natural hot spring sacred to the Romano-Celtic goddess Sulis Minerva — already, by Trajan's reign, drawing pilgrims and invalids to its temple and bathing complex.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Roman Baths in Bath Spa, England - July 2006.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: The Roman Baths at Aquae Sulis, Bath · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Great Bath at the Roman Baths, Bath

properties.name: Corinium Dobunnorum
properties.notes: Modern Cirencester, Gloucestershire — civitas capital of the Dobunni and, by the later Roman period, the second-largest town in Britain after Londinium, sitting at the crossing of the Fosse Way and Ermin Street.
properties.image_credit: Earthworks of the Roman amphitheatre at Corinium Dobunnorum, Cirencester · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Grass-covered amphitheatre earthworks at Cirencester

properties.name: Ratae Corieltauvorum
properties.notes: Modern Leicester — civitas capital of the Corieltauvi, with a forum-basilica complex and public baths whose Jewry Wall still stands among the tallest surviving Roman masonry in Britain.
properties.image_credit: The Jewry Wall, a surviving Roman bathhouse wall at Ratae Corieltauvorum, Leicester · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Jewry Wall Roman masonry in Leicester

properties.name: Vernemetum
properties.notes: A roadside settlement at Willoughby-on-the-Wolds, Nottinghamshire, whose Brittonic name means 'great sacred grove' — a shared node linking the Fosse Way toward the Ermine Street corridor further east.

properties.name: Margidunum
properties.notes: A defended way-station at East Bridgford/Bingham, Nottinghamshire, with its own ditched fortification — the Fosse Way here ran close enough to hostile territory in the early conquest period to need real defenses, not just an open mansio.

properties.name: Ad Pontem
properties.notes: A fort and way-station at East Stoke, Nottinghamshire, guarding the Fosse Way's crossing of the River Trent — its very name simply means 'at the bridge.'

properties.name: Crococalana
properties.notes: A mansio near Brough, Nottinghamshire, the last stop on the Fosse Way before it met the Ermine Street corridor and the colonia at Lindum — a genuine road junction as well as a rest station.

properties.name: Corstopitum
properties.notes: Modern Corbridge, Northumberland — the Stanegate's eastern anchor and one of the largest fort-and-supply-base sites on the northern frontier, where the Stanegate met Dere Street running up from York. Granaries built here to provision Trajan's northern garrisons still stand.
properties.image_credit: Excavated street remains at Corstopitum, Corbridge · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman street remains at Corbridge

properties.name: Newbrough
properties.notes: A small fortlet on the Stanegate west of Corbridge, under an acre in size — one of the modest garrison posts strung along this pre-Wall frontier road roughly every few miles.
properties.image_credit: The Stanegate at Newbrough · Wikimedia Commons (Geograph)
properties.image_alt: The route of the Roman Stanegate road passing Newbrough, site of a small Roman fort on the frontier road.

properties.name: Haltwhistle Burn
properties.notes: A small fortlet above the Haltwhistle Burn in Northumberland, part of the same close-set chain of minor posts along the Stanegate that would later inform the spacing of milecastles on Hadrian's Wall.

properties.name: Magnis
properties.notes: The fort at Carvoran, Northumberland, guarding the point where the Stanegate crosses the Maiden Way running north from the Pennines — a genuine road-junction garrison, not just a way-station.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Carvoran (Magna) Roman Fort - tower at northwest corner (2) - geograph.org.uk - 1374211.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Corner tower remains at Magnis (Carvoran) Roman fort · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Stone tower foundations at Carvoran fort

properties.name: Nether Denton
properties.notes: A fort and attached civilian vicus at Nether Denton, Cumbria, on the Stanegate's approach to the Irthing valley — one of the string of garrisons holding this frontier road two decades before Hadrian's Wall existed.

properties.name: Boothby
properties.notes: A small fortlet near Brampton, Cumbria, sized for a handful of soldiers rather than a full garrison — a change-of-horses post rather than a fighting position.

properties.name: Brampton Old Church
properties.notes: A fort controlling the Stanegate's crossing of the River Irthing near Brampton, Cumbria — command of this river crossing made it one of the more substantial posts on the road's western stretch.

properties.name: Luguvalium
properties.notes: Modern Carlisle, Cumbria — the Stanegate's western terminus and, within a few years of Trajan's death, capital of the whole northern frontier zone. A fort had stood here since the Flavian conquest of the north, decades before Hadrian's Wall was ever planned.
properties.image_credit: Roman-era artefacts from Luguvalium (Carlisle), Tullie House Museum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman artefacts on display at Tullie House

properties.name: Eboracum
properties.notes: Modern York — headquarters fortress of Legio IX Hispana and then Legio VI Victrix, and Ermine Street's northern terminus. By 117 CE it was already the military and administrative center of the whole northern frontier.
properties.image_credit: The Multangular Tower, surviving corner of the Eboracum (York) legionary fortress walls, Legio IX Hispana base · Wikimedia Commons (reused, same site as poi_fortress_ix_hispana_eboracum)

properties.name: Petuaria
properties.notes: Modern Brough-on-Humber, East Yorkshire — a civitas center for the Parisi and a Humber-crossing point, on an alternate branch of the road network linking Eboracum toward Lincoln.
properties.image_credit: Petuaria finds, Hull and East Riding Museum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman-era finds from Petuaria (Brough-on-Humber) on display at the Hull and East Riding Museum.

properties.name: Legeolium
properties.notes: A fort and mansio at modern Castleford, West Yorkshire, where Ermine Street crossed the River Aire — the fort guarded the crossing while the mansio served travelers on the York-Lincoln road.

properties.name: Danum
properties.notes: Modern Doncaster, South Yorkshire — a fort and mansio on Ermine Street's crossing of the River Don, part of the chain of garrisons securing the road between York and Lincoln.
properties.image_credit: The Danum shield, a 1st-century Roman shield excavated at the Danum fort/station site, Doncaster · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Segelocum
properties.notes: A mansio at Littleborough, Nottinghamshire, where Ermine Street forded the River Trent — the crossing itself, more than any settlement, is what put a station here.

properties.name: Lindum Colonia
properties.notes: Modern Lincoln — a legionary fortress converted into a colonia for army veterans, and the meeting point of Ermine Street with the Fosse Way running southwest toward Exeter. One of only four such veteran coloniae in Roman Britain.
properties.image_credit: Newport Arch, the surviving Roman gate of Lindum Colonia, Lincoln · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman Newport Arch in Lincoln

properties.name: Ad Savonem (Safo fl.)
properties.notes: The Tabula Peutingeriana marks the Via Domitiana's crossing of the river Savo only as "Safo fl." (the river itself), about 7 Roman miles south of Sinuessa — a different crossing from the well-known Pons Campanus, which carries the inland Via Appia over the same river near Casilinum. No bridge structure or exact ford has been pinpointed archaeologically for this crossing; the point given here is an approximate placement near the modern Savone river mouth.
sources: Tabula Peutingeriana, Segment VI (K. Miller, Itineraria Romana, entry 347, "Safo fl.")
Statius, Silvae 4.3 (river-crossing context of the road)

properties.name: Pons Vulturni (bridge over the Volturnus)
properties.notes: The Via Domitiana's centerpiece engineering feat, a bridge over the Volturnus near its mouth that Statius personifies and celebrates at length — the river-god Vulturnus boasts of finally "carrying a bridge" instead of scattering into marshy fords, a passage written to mark the road's 95 CE dedication. The adjoining Roman colonia of Volturnum (founded 194 BCE) grew up beside the crossing; masonry from the Roman bridge was later reused as the base of the medieval Castel Volturno fortress on the same spot.

properties.name: Liternum
properties.notes: A Roman colonia founded in 194 BCE on the coastal plain between the Volturnus mouth and Cumae, which the new Via Domitiana ran directly through in 95 CE. Scipio Africanus retired here after his political fall and was buried nearby, a detail Seneca later used the town to reflect on — giving the road's route through Liternum a literary weight beyond its role as a waystation.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Liternum, Lago Patria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ancient Roman ruins at Liternum near Lago Patria, on the Via Domitiana

properties.name: In Vineis
properties.notes: A minor waystation — the name means "among the vineyards" — recorded on the Tabula Peutingeriana between Cumae and Puteoli, generally identified with the site of Arco Felice, where Domitian's engineers cut a dramatic passage through the hill of Monte Grillo to carry the road toward Puteoli. The still-standing arch there (Arco Felice Vecchio, roughly 20m tall) is one of the road's clearest surviving monuments.
sources: Tabula Peutingeriana, Segment VI (K. Miller, Itineraria Romana)
archeoflegrei.it, "I Campi Flegrei nella Tabula Peutingeriana"

properties.name: Antiochia Caesarea
properties.notes: The caput viae — every milestone on the Via Sebaste counted its distance from this Augustan colony. Refounded as a Roman veteran settlement and used as the region's main garrison and administrative base, Antioch anchored the road the governor Cornutus Arruntius Aquila built in 6 BCE to move troops quickly against the Taurus hill tribes and down to the Pamphylian coast.
properties.image_credit: Antioch of Pisidia (Antiochia Caesarea), street from the West Gate · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the colonnaded street near the West Gate at Antioch of Pisidia, the terminus of the Via Sebaste.

properties.name: Apollonia
properties.notes: A Hellenistic foundation in Pisidia (earlier called Mordiaeon) that the Via Sebaste's Augustan builders folded into the new road network as the first major stop southwest of Antioch, on the stretch that swung the route toward Lake Burdur and Comama. No individual milestone distance from Antioch survives for this stretch.

properties.name: Comama
properties.notes: An Augustan veteran colony (Colonia Iulia Augusta Prima Fida Comama), one of five planted around Antioch in 6 BCE to pin down the Pisidian mountain tribes. An Augustan milestone found on the site itself reads CXXII — 122 Roman miles from Antioch, the road's caput viae, which this figure reflects rather than a distance from Apollonia specifically. Here the road split: one branch ran west to Olbasa, another southeast to Cremna, and the mainline continued south through the Climax Pass to Perge.

properties.name: Olbasa
properties.notes: A western branch off the Via Sebaste at Comama, roughly 25-30 km away (no surviving milestone gives an exact figure). Another of Augustus's Pisidian veteran colonies, titled Colonia Iulia Augusta like its sister foundations, planted to extend Roman control and road access into the western highlands.

properties.name: Cremna
properties.notes: A southeastern branch off the Via Sebaste at Comama, roughly 35 km away (no surviving milestone gives an exact figure). Perched on a defensible plateau above the Cestrus river gorge, Cremna was garrisoned by Augustan veterans as a forward post against the Homonadensian tribes; a century after its founding it withstood a dramatic siege by the rebel Lydius against a Roman relief force, an episode Strabo records.

properties.name: Mansio in Klimax
properties.notes: The best-preserved Roman mansio in all of Asia Minor, still standing to roof height in the Doseme Bogazi pass with a courtyard, nine ground-floor rooms for pack animals and six upper rooms for travelers. An Augustan milestone beside it reads CXXXIX — 139 Roman miles from Antioch, 17 past Comama's own CXXII marker — fixing the mansio at the road's critical Taurus Mountains chokepoint between the Pisidian plateau and the Pamphylian coast. Coordinates are an approximate placement for the pass; no public exact figure was found for the mansio building itself.
sources: Mitchell, Wagner & Williams (2021), Roman Archaeology in a South Anatolian Landscape: The Via Sebaste, the Mansio in the Doseme Bogazi, and Regional Transhumance in Pamphylia and Pisidia, Koc University Press

properties.name: Perge
properties.notes: The Via Sebaste's Mediterranean end point, giving Rome's inland Pisidian colonies a direct paved route to a Pamphylian port. Acts 13 places Paul and Barnabas landing and later re-embarking here, almost certainly using this same road on their inland leg to Pisidian Antioch. A 2008 survey documented a newly-identified stretch of the road and its roadside buildings running from here up to the Climax Pass.
properties.image_credit: Perge, Roman thermae, Palaestra · Wikimedia Commons (reused, same site as sport_gymnasium_perge)
properties.image_alt: Palaestra rooms of the Roman baths and gymnasium at Perge

properties.name: Ad Sorores
properties.notes: First overnight halt heading north out of Emerita Augusta on the road to Asturica, roughly where the modern village of Casas de Don Antonio now stands.

properties.name: Castra Caecilia
properties.notes: A former Republican-era army camp on the Ribera del Marco springs, later a road station serving the site that grew into modern Caceres.

properties.name: Turmulus
properties.notes: Marked the crossing of the Tagus at Alconetar, where a Roman bridge carried the road over the river near modern Garrovillas de Alconetar.

properties.name: Rusticiana
properties.notes: A waystation on the plain north of the Tagus, generally placed at modern Galisteo, walled centuries later on the same defensible river bend.

properties.name: Capara
properties.notes: A full Roman town, not just a waystation, with its own forum, baths and an amphitheater. Its four-faced arch still stands astride the old road between Guijo de Granadilla and Oliva de Plasencia, the best-preserved monument on the entire route.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Caparra, Extremadura · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Caecilius Vicus
properties.notes: A roadside settlement at the southern foot of the mountain pass into the Duero basin, on the site of the hot springs at modern Banos de Montemayor.

properties.name: Ad Lippos
properties.notes: A short relay stage climbing through the Sierra de Bejar pass; no excavated remains confirm the exact spot, and the village of La Calzada de Bejar preserves only the road's name, not a proven station site.

properties.name: Sentice
properties.notes: The highest point of the whole road between Emerita and Asturica, somewhere in the hills around modern Fuenterroble de Salvatierra. Archaeologists are still searching for its exact footprint.

properties.name: Salmantica
properties.notes: A walled hilltop town on the Tormes, already old when Hannibal besieged it in 220 BCE. In 117 CE it is a working stop on the imperial road, not yet the university city its Roman bridge still carries traffic toward today.

properties.name: Sibarim
properties.notes: Recorded as sitting almost exactly halfway between Salmantica and Ocelo Duri, in open country north of Salamanca near modern Calzada de Valdunciel, but with no confirmed archaeological footprint.

properties.name: Ocelo Duri
properties.notes: Named for its position on the Duero, "the Eye of the Duero," near where the Romans defeated the Lusitanian leader Viriathus. Excavated road remains survive near modern Villalazan, Zamora.

properties.name: Albocela
properties.notes: A Vaccaei-territory station on the Duero's north bank, generally but not conclusively placed under modern Toro; distance here is estimated from the road's known path rather than a surviving itinerary figure.

properties.name: Amallobriga
properties.notes: A station on the open Tierra de Campos plain, tentatively placed near modern Tiedra though the identification is disputed among Spanish archaeologists; distance estimated from the road's known path.

properties.name: Brigaecium
properties.notes: An Astures-territory town on the last stretch before Asturica Augusta, independently recorded as 40 Roman miles from that city. Its remains sit at the Penon de Villabrazaro, near Benavente.

properties.name: Vodgoriacum
properties.notes: A vicus at modern Waudrez, near Binche, on the stretch of road running north out of Bavay toward Tongeren. Excavation has confirmed continuous Roman-period occupation here, matching the Antonine Itinerary's placement between Bagacum and Geminiacum.

properties.name: Geminiacum
properties.notes: One of the best-excavated vici on the whole Bavay-Cologne road, at Liberchies in modern Pont-a-Celles, dug systematically since 1956. Coin finds there run continuously through the Roman period, confirming it as a real working roadside settlement rather than a guess from the text alone.

properties.name: Perniciacum
properties.notes: A vicus at modern Braives, named Pernaco on the Peutinger Table and Perniciacum in the Antonine Itinerary, on the long stretch of road between Liberchies and Tongeren.

properties.name: Aduaca Tungrorum
properties.notes: Civitas capital of the Tungri, at modern Tongeren, the largest town on this stretch of Gallia Belgica and still ringed today by its Roman-era walls. The road crossed here on its way to the Rhine frontier.
properties.image_credit: Fragment of the Roman city walls of Aduaca Tungrorum (Tongeren) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman wall fragment in Tongeren

properties.name: Coriovallum
properties.notes: A road-junction settlement at modern Heerlen, where this road met the north-south route linking the Rhine legionary bases. Excavated bathhouse remains are still on public display beneath the modern town center.
properties.image_credit: Excavated Roman bathhouse of Coriovallum (Heerlen), Thermenmuseum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman bathhouse excavation in Heerlen

properties.name: Iuliacum
properties.notes: A vicus at modern Julich, the last waystation before the road reached the Rhine at Cologne. Its name survives almost unchanged into the modern German town.

properties.name: Colonia Agrippina
properties.notes: This branch's eastern terminus at the Rhine, modern Cologne, seat of the governor of Germania Inferior and home port of the Rhine fleet. The road tied Britannia's Channel crossing directly to this legionary frontier in one continuous line, closing out the Bavay-Cologne stretch of Via Agrippa's northern network.
properties.image_credit: Reconstructed Roman city gate arch of Colonia Agrippina (Cologne) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Reconstructed Roman arch in Cologne

properties.name: Thantia
properties.notes: A station on the Peutinger Table's Bostra-to-Hatita stretch of the Via Traiana Nova, tentatively placed near Thughrat el-Jubb. Its Peutinger mileage (24 Roman miles from Bostra, 9 more to Hatita) does not fully reconcile with Hatita's own recorded distance from Bostra elsewhere in this file, so treat the exact figures as unsettled alongside the identification. Coordinates are interpolated along the road line between Bostra and Hatita, not a surveyed find-spot.

properties.name: Ad Dianam
properties.notes: A minor waystation, likely named for a roadside shrine to Diana, on the Peutinger Table's Via Traiana Nova sequence between Praesidium and Aila (Aqaba) at the road's southern end. The 16-Roman-mile distance from Aila recurs consistently across sources; the distance reported from Praesidium's side conflicts between different readings and is left unrecorded here rather than guessed. Coordinates are interpolated along the road line between Praesidium and Aila, not a surveyed find-spot. Not to be confused with an unrelated same-named station on the Via Egnatia in Albania.

properties.name: Esbus
properties.notes: Esbus (biblical Heshbon) sat on the Via Nova Traiana at its junction with the Roman road running west to Livias, Jericho and Jerusalem. Modern Tell Hisban has been excavated since 1968 by the Heshbon Expedition, which uncovered Roman-Byzantine occupation and several milestones from the adjoining Esbus-Livias road.
sources: Blue Guide Jordan, entry for Hesban (Heshbon)
'The Work of the Heshbon Survey Team, 1973', Ministry Magazine (1974)
properties.image_credit: Roman column, Tell Hesban (ancient Esbus) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman-era column at Tell Hesban, site of ancient Esbus

properties.name: Medaba
properties.notes: Medaba (modern Madaba) was a sizeable Roman-Byzantine town on the Via Nova Traiana between Esbus and the Wadi Mujib/Arnon crossing toward Rabbathmoba. Its 6th-century mosaic floor map in the Church of St George is the principal ancient visual record of this road's towns.
sources: D.F. Graf, 'The Via Nova Traiana in Arabia Petraea', in The Roman and Byzantine Near East, JRA Supplementary Series 14
properties.image_credit: Mosaic, Church of the Apostles, Madaba (ancient Medaba) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Byzantine mosaic inside the Church of the Apostles at Madaba

properties.name: Dibon
properties.notes: Dibon (modern Dhiban), the old Moabite capital, lay on the Via Nova Traiana immediately north of the Wadi Mujib (ancient Arnon) gorge, where the Roman road descended in switchbacks alongside the Iron Age sites of Dhiban, Aroer and Lehun to cross toward Rabbathmoba/Areopolis.
sources: 'Making Peoples: The Nabataean Settlement of the Dhiban Plateau and Beyond' (ResearchGate)
properties.image_credit: Ancient ruins at Dhiban, site of Roman-era Dibon · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Close-up of the ancient ruins at Dhiban, Jordan

properties.name: Arindela
properties.notes: Arindela (modern Gharandal, Tafilah Governorate, 15 km southeast of Tafilah) had a late-Nabataean or early Roman monumental stone complex, probably a caravanserai, later overbuilt by a Byzantine church. A 2nd-century Latin funerary inscription found there names a soldier of a cohors Ulpia miliaria, evidence of a Trajanic-era garrison on this stretch of the road.
sources: 'A New Latin Funerary Inscription from Gharandal (Southern Jordan)' (academia.edu)
'The Church at Arindela (Gharandal) of Palaestina Tertia' (ResearchGate)

properties.name: Khirbet al-Tabieh
properties.notes: Field survey traced the main Trajanic roadbed running along the west side of Khirbet al-Tabieh as it descends the Ras al-Naqab escarpment toward Humayma (Hauarra); no ancient name for the site is preserved. Coordinates are an approximate placement on the escarpment descent between Zadagatta and Hauarra, pending precise survey coordinates.
sources: F. Abudanah & S. Twaissi, 'The Via Nova Traiana Between Petra and Ayn Al-Qana In Arabia Petraea', Oxford Journal of Archaeology 35(1), 2016

properties.name: Rujm Ayn al-Qana
properties.notes: A 6x6 m watchtower at Rujm Ayn al-Qana commands the line of the Via Nova Traiana from the lower slopes of the Ras al-Naqab escarpment down to Humayma (Hauarra) and its aqueduct, implying a small detachment guarded this segment of road. No ancient name is attested; its position here is an approximate placement along the escarpment route, pending precise survey coordinates.
sources: F. Abudanah & S. Twaissi, 'The Via Nova Traiana Between Petra and Ayn Al-Qana In Arabia Petraea', Oxford Journal of Archaeology 35(1), 2016

properties.name: Eboracum
properties.notes: The fortress of Legio VI Victrix and headquarters of the whole northern command, where Dere Street began its 156-mile run to Bremenium and the far frontier. Roads radiated from here in every direction, but this one carried troops and supplies straight up the eastern flank of the Pennines toward the future line of Hadrian's Wall.
properties.image_credit: The Multangular Tower, surviving corner of the Eboracum (York) legionary fortress walls, Legio IX Hispana base · Wikimedia Commons (reused, same site as poi_fortress_ix_hispana_eboracum)

properties.name: Isurium Brigantum
properties.notes: A market settlement of the Brigantes at modern Aldborough, where Dere Street crossed the River Ure 17 Roman miles north of York. It would later grow into the tribe's civitas capital, but under Trajan it was still a working roadside town serving travelers and troops bound for the frontier.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Mosaic depicting the She-wolf with Romulus and Remus, from Aldborough, about 300-400 AD, Leeds City Museum (16025914306).jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: She-wolf mosaic from Isurium Brigantum (Aldborough), now in Leeds City Museum — a museum artifact from the site, not an on-site view · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman mosaic of the she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus

properties.name: Scotch Corner settlement
properties.notes: A trading settlement at the junction where Dere Street met the road running west toward Carlisle over Stainmore. It was founded a decade before the Roman conquest even reached Yorkshire and flourished for only 20 to 30 years before its trade and population shifted south to the new town at Cataractonium. By Trajan's reign the site had stood empty for decades.

properties.name: Healam Bridge
properties.notes: A roadside settlement where Dere Street crossed Healam Beck, roughly midway between Aldborough and Catterick. The road itself had run through here since the late 1st century, but the settlement that grew up beside it is usually dated to the start of Hadrian's reign, just after this snapshot, when it expanded into an 18-hectare spread of timber workshops and yards.

properties.name: Cataractonium
properties.notes: A fort-and-town complex where Dere Street bridged the River Swale, 24 Roman miles north of Aldborough. Founded in 71 CE by governor Quintus Petillius Cerialis, it had grown into a busy leatherworking and supply center for the northern garrisons by Trajan's reign, with enough literate staff on hand to leave behind hundreds of writing styli.

properties.name: Bainesse
properties.notes: A satellite settlement two kilometers southeast of Cataractonium, founded under the Flavian emperors as a hub for blacksmiths, bronze-workers and potters serving Dere Street traffic. Its kiln is the only one positively identified anywhere in the Catterick area, and by Trajan's reign stone buildings had begun replacing the original timber ones.

properties.name: Vinovia
properties.notes: The largest Roman fort in County Durham, raised around 79 CE on a hilltop above the River Wear, 22 Roman miles north of Catterick. Its garrison guarded Dere Street's crossing of the Wear, and centuries later the site would yield the best-preserved Roman military bathhouse found anywhere in Britain.
properties.image_credit: Photograph via Wikimedia Commons (reused, same site as poi_auxfort_vinovia)

properties.name: Vindomora
properties.notes: A fort at modern Ebchester, built when Dere Street was pushed north from York to Corbridge around 80 CE, 19 Roman miles beyond Binchester. It held roughly 500 auxiliary troops and served as an overnight staging post on the northern road for more than three centuries.

properties.name: Corstopitum
properties.notes: The Stanegate's eastern anchor and Dere Street's last major stop before the frontier, nine Roman miles north of Ebchester at the lowest fordable point of the Tyne. By Trajan's death it was already a major supply base and arsenal for the northern army, four decades before Hadrian's Wall was even planned.
properties.image_credit: Excavated street remains at Corstopitum, Corbridge (reused, same site as station_corstopitum) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman street remains at Corbridge

properties.name: Bremenium
properties.notes: The northernmost stop named in the Antonine Itinerary's British road list, 20 Roman miles beyond Corbridge, with a turf-and-timber fort that Trajan's engineers modified in his final years. Excavated pottery shows no occupation here during Hadrian's reign, so whatever garrison held it at Trajan's death did not stay much longer.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Archaeology excavation near Bremenium Roman Fort - geograph.org.uk - 6908416.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Archaeological excavation near Bremenium Roman fort, High Rochester · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Excavation trench near Bremenium fort

properties.name: Chew Green
properties.notes: A cluster of marching camps, fortlets and a permanent fort where Dere Street crossed the headwaters of the River Coquet, about eight miles north of Bremenium. Its ancient name is disputed, with proposed identifications including Ad Fines and Uysela from the Ravenna Cosmography. The Flavian-period fortlet here had gone out of use before Trajan died, part of the broader pull-back from the far side of the Cheviots.
properties.image_credit: Earthworks of the Roman camp complex at Chew Green · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman camp earthworks at Chew Green

properties.name: Cappuck
properties.notes: A small bridgehead fort on the east bank of the Oxnam Water, guarding Dere Street's crossing 11 miles southeast of Newstead. Excavation found two Flavian-Trajanic occupation layers followed by a long gap before the site was rebuilt around 140 CE, so its garrison had already pulled out by the time Trajan died.

properties.name: Trimontium
properties.notes: The most heavily fortified Roman position north of the Cheviots, built by Agricola below the three peaks of the Eildon Hills to control Dere Street's crossing of the Tweed. Fire damage and scattered weapons found in its ditches point to real fighting around 105 CE, when Rome abandoned the fort and pulled its northern garrisons back toward the Tyne-Solway line, a dozen years before this snapshot.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre earthworks at Trimontium, Newstead · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman amphitheatre remains at Trimontium

properties.name: Oxton fortlet
properties.notes: A small fortlet on a ridge above Dere Street in the Lammermuir Hills, guarding the road's push north toward the Forth beyond Trimontium. One of its four attached annexes stretched 225 meters along the roadside, but excavation found nothing to suggest occupation survived the pullback that emptied Trimontium and the rest of the Flavian-Trajanic garrison network to its south.

properties.name: Elginhaugh
properties.notes: A Flavian fort at the North Esk crossing near Dalkeith, the most completely excavated timber auxiliary fort found anywhere in the Roman Empire. Coin evidence dates its short life to about 79 to 87 CE, after which it was deliberately dismantled — three decades before Trajan even took the throne, let alone died.

properties.name: Ad Nonum
properties.notes: Ad Nonum sat at the ninth Roman mile out of the city, where the Via Praenestina crossed a ravine on the seven-arch Ponte di Nona bridge. Excavations here in 1975 and 1976 uncovered a Republican-era rural healing sanctuary that had produced more than 8,000 terracotta votive offerings, many shaped as afflicted hands and feet, before the site was largely destroyed by pozzolana quarrying in the 1960s. The Barrington Atlas records it as a named road station on the stretch before Gabii.
sources: Barrington Atlas of the Greek and Roman World, Map 43 (Latium Vetus)
Potter, T.W. and Wells, C., 'A Republican Healing-Sanctuary at Ponte di Nona near Rome', Journal of the British Archaeological Association 138 (1985)

properties.name: Ad Vacanas (Baccanae)
properties.notes: Travelers heading north from Rome reached this posting station in the Baccano valley at the 21st milestone, where the road split: the Via Cassia carried on into Etruria while the Via Amerina turned off toward Falerii and Umbria. Excavations at Baccano uncovered a paved stretch of the ancient road alongside remains of the mansio itself. The station sat inside an extinct volcanic crater, its rim still visible in the surrounding farmland.

properties.name: Nepet (Nepi)
properties.notes: Nepi was the first Faliscan town the Via Amerina reached, an Etruscan hill settlement Rome turned into a Latin colony in the fourth century BCE. The road hit it nine Roman miles beyond the Baccano junction, and its catacombs and Roman-era aqueduct still trace the ancient layout. Deep gorges wrap three sides of the town, the same natural defenses that made it worth holding.
properties.image_credit: Roman aqueduct at Nepi · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ancient Roman aqueduct arches at Nepi

properties.name: Ponte Romano dei Tre Ponti
properties.notes: A short way north of Nepi, the Via Amerina crossed the Fosso dei Tre Ponti on a Roman bridge that still carries the deep wheel ruts of the ancient roadbed. Faliscan and Roman-era tombs cut into the tufa cliffs line both banks of the stream. It's one of the best-preserved single-span crossings surviving anywhere on the road.

properties.name: Falerii Novi
properties.notes: Rome resettled the defeated Falisci here in 241 BCE after razing their hilltop capital, and the new town rose along the road with its own forum, theater, and baths. Its walls, still standing nearly to full height, enclose fifty hectares that no later town ever built over. The Porta di Giove gate ranks among the best-preserved Republican-era city gates in Italy.
properties.image_credit: Porta di Giove, Falerii Novi · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman city gate and walls of Falerii Novi

properties.name: Falerii Veteres (Civita Castellana)
properties.notes: The old Faliscan capital lost its population when Rome forced the move to Falerii Novi in 241 BCE, but the site didn't go empty. The sanctuary of Juno Curitis in the valley below kept drawing worshippers well into the imperial period, and a small settlement lingered on the tufa plateau that later became Civita Castellana, just off the Via Amerina's course.
properties.image_credit: Forte Sangallo, built on the ancient Falerii Veteres acropolis · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Fortress standing on the plateau of ancient Falerii Veteres

properties.name: Fescennium
properties.notes: One of the Falisci's principal towns stood on the plateau just north of modern Corchiano, inside the branch of the Via Amerina that ran through Faliscan territory. Ancient writers credited the place as the source of the coarse fescennine verses sung at Roman weddings and harvests. Its ruins remain unexcavated, known mainly through tomb finds in the surrounding ravines.

properties.name: Castellum Amerinum
properties.notes: Twelve Roman miles past Falerii, the road reached a fortified landing on the Tiber that handled traffic and goods bound upstream toward Umbria. The Tabula Peutingeriana marks it as Castellum Amerinum, a walled post between Falerii Novi and Ameria, but which riverside village holds the actual remains is still argued over. Bassano in Teverina and the Palazzolo district of Vasanello both claim the identification.

properties.name: Horta (Orte)
properties.notes: Orte's Etruscan hilltop, ringed on three sides by river gorges, became a stop on the Via Amerina as the road ran up the Tiber's left bank before crossing over into Umbria. Roman armies had already fought twice near here for control of the crossing against Etruscan Volsinii before the town's fortunes turned to trade and travel. The medieval hill town still occupies the same defensible perch the Romans valued.

properties.name: Ameria (Amelia)
properties.notes: Ameria gave the whole road its name and sat fifty-five Roman miles from Rome by the Peutinger Table's count, the first Umbrian town the Via Amerina reached. Its walls of massive uncemented polygonal blocks, still standing over six meters high in places, predate the Roman conquest by centuries. Cicero defended a local client from here in one of his earliest surviving courtroom speeches.
properties.image_credit: Polygonal walls of Amelia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Massive pre-Roman polygonal wall blocks at Amelia

properties.name: Tuder (Todi)
properties.notes: North of Amelia the road climbed to Tuder, an Umbrian hill town Rome elevated to colony status under Augustus as Colonia Julia Fida Tuder. Its temples and forum crowned one of the most commanding sites on the whole route, visible for miles across the Tiber valley. From here the Via Amerina kept climbing north toward Perugia.
properties.image_credit: View of Todi · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Hilltop town of Todi in Umbria

properties.name: Vettona (Bettona)
properties.notes: Bettona sits on a ridge above the Chiascio and Topino rivers, an Umbrian hill town the Via Amerina's northern extension reached on the final stretch toward Perugia. Rome absorbed it as a municipium in the fourth century BCE, and Pliny the Elder later counted it among Umbria's fifteen recognized peoples. Etruscan-style walls still ring the old town center.

properties.name: Nomentum
properties.notes: Nomentum crowned a low ridge fourteen and a half Roman miles up the Via Nomentana, the market town that gave the road its name and its endpoint. Tuff-block walls from the fourth century BCE still trace its old acropolis on Montedoro hill above modern Mentana. Strabo placed it on the road linking Rome to the Sabine country, and the poet Martial owned a farm nearby he wrote about constantly. Rome absorbed it as a subject town with limited citizenship after 338 BCE.
properties.image_credit: General view of Mentana, built over ancient Nomentum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View of the modern town of Mentana on the site of ancient Nomentum

properties.name: Ponte Nomentano
properties.notes: The Via Nomentana crossed the Aniene here on a stone bridge built around 100 BCE, not quite four kilometers past Rome's northern gate. The Ostrogothic king Totila tore it down in 547 CE during the siege of Rome, and the general Narses rebuilt it five years later once the city was retaken. A squat medieval tower still guards the crossing today, standing on Roman arches laid some six centuries before it. It was the first landmark travelers passed leaving Rome for Sabine country.
properties.image_credit: Ponte Nomentano, the Roman-and-medieval bridge over the Aniene · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ponte Nomentano bridge with its medieval tower over the Aniene river

properties.name: Ad Nonas (Settecamini)
properties.notes: A milestone reading IX from Rome gave this post station its name, Ad Nonas, roughly halfway along the Via Tiburtina to Tibur. Archaeologists uncovered it in 1951 at Settecamini: a portico onto a paved courtyard, a well, and a semicircular corridor built for fast horse changes. Floor mosaics and reticulate brickwork date the complex to the first century BCE, with use continuing into the fifth. A long stretch of the original basalt paving survives beside it, still rutted from cart wheels.
properties.image_credit: The Via Tiburtina near Rome · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The modern Via Tiburtina roadway near Rome, tracing the ancient route

properties.name: Ponte Lucano
properties.notes: This seven-arched bridge carried the Via Tiburtina over the Aniene at the road's fourteenth Roman mile, right where travelers made their final climb into Tibur. Its neighbor is the drum-shaped Tomb of the Plautii, raised in the first century BCE, whose own inscriptions are sometimes wrongly credited to the bridge itself. The span carried traffic without a break into the twentieth century, its Roman core still standing under later medieval rebuilding.
properties.image_credit: Ponte Lucano over the Aniene, with the Tomb of the Plautii · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ponte Lucano Roman bridge and the round Tomb of the Plautii

properties.name: Hatria (Adria)
properties.notes: Hatria anchored the southern end of the Via Annia, the road praetor Titus Annius Rufus cut north to Aquileia in 131 BCE. The old Adriatic port, once Etruscan and Greek, gave the sea itself its name. From here the new road struck north across the Po delta toward Patavium, 25 unattested miles away.

properties.name: Patavium (Padua)
properties.notes: Patavium was the wealthiest city in Cisalpine Gaul, and the Via Annia used it as the pivot point for its final 82-mile push to Aquileia. The historian Livy was born within its walls. No ancient itinerary records a named station on the 25-mile stretch south to Adria, leaving that leg of the road undocumented by name.

properties.name: Mansio ad Duodecimum (Sambruson)
properties.notes: Ad Duodecimum took its name straight from its distance: 12 Roman miles north of Padua. Travelers changed horses here, at the exact spot where the Meduacus river forked and where the Via Annia met the coastal road running down from Ravenna. A milestone naming Constantine, unearthed at Sambruson in 1887, shows the post still worked four centuries after the road was cut.
sources: Itin. Burd. 560,4 (mutatio ad Duodecimum, XII m.p.)

properties.name: Mutatio ad Nonum (Marghera)
properties.notes: Ad Nonum sat 9 Roman miles short of Altinum, on the marshy shoreline that later became the industrial port of Marghera. The Itinerarium Burdigalense lists it as a bare mutatio, a horse-change stop with no town attached to it. Travelers passed through on a raised roadbed built to survive the lagoon floods.
sources: Itin. Burd. 560,5 (mutatio ad Nonum, XI m.p.)

properties.name: Altinum
properties.notes: Altinum was a thriving lagoon port where the Via Annia met ferry routes into the islands that later became Venice. Wealthy Roman villas lined its canals, and the town's own coinage circulated across the northern Adriatic. Its final approach from Marghera ran 9 Roman miles along an embanked causeway built to outlast the marsh.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons contributor
properties.image_alt: Paved remains of the Via Annia within the archaeological area of Altinum

properties.name: Piave Crossing Milestones (Ceggia)
properties.notes: Multiple imperial-era milestones turned up around Ceggia, marking where the Via Annia crossed the Piave river on its way to Concordia. One names Caesar Flavius Julius Crispus, son of Constantine, who held that title for less than a decade before his execution in 326 CE. Others honor Valentinian, Theodosius and Arcadius, evidence the crossing stayed in repair for four centuries.

properties.name: Mutatio Sanos
properties.notes: Mutatio Sanos marked the Via Annia's crossing of the Livenza river, 10 Roman miles past Altinum on the road to Concordia. The Itinerarium Burdigalense records it as nothing more than a horse-change post, one of the anonymous relay stops that kept the cursus publicus running. Modern scholarship places it near Sant'Anastasio, a hamlet that still sits beside the river.

properties.name: Iulia Concordia (Concordia Sagittaria)
properties.notes: Iulia Concordia grew out of a Via Annia relay station roughly midway between Altinum and Aquileia, then became a full Roman colony in 42 BCE. The road entered town over a bridge whose stone piers still stand today. Sitting at the junction with the Via Postumia, Concordia funneled traffic between the Alps, the Adriatic and Aquileia.
sources: Itin. Burd. 560,8 (civitas Iulia Concordia, VIIII m.p.)
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons contributor
properties.image_alt: Paved section of the Via Annia preserved at Iulia Concordia

properties.name: Mutatio Apicilia (Latisanotta)
properties.notes: Mutatio Apicilia, also transmitted as ad Paciliam, sat 9 Roman miles east of Concordia at a crossing on a minor branch of the Tagliamento. The stop survives today in the hamlet name Latisanotta, still perched by the same river ford it once guarded. Like most mutationes on this stretch it existed for one job: swapping tired horses for the cursus publicus.

properties.name: Palazzolo dello Stella Milestones
properties.notes: A cluster of Roman milestones turned up around Palazzolo dello Stella, including one dedicated to Constantine after 312 CE. The finds mark a well-maintained stretch of the Via Annia's final approach to Aquileia, where the road crossed the marshy delta of the Stella river. Additional milestones nearby name later fourth-century emperors, showing the route stayed under active repair for generations.

properties.name: Mutatio ad Undecimum (Chiarisacco)
properties.notes: Mutatio ad Undecimum stood exactly 11 Roman miles from Aquileia, at the site now called Chiarisacco near Malisana. Excavators recovered five milestones there, including two naming co-emperors Valentinian and Valens and one naming the usurper Magnentius. That dense cluster of inscriptions makes it one of the best-documented relay points on the whole road.
sources: Itin. Burd. 560,10 (mutatio ad Undecimum, XI m.p.)

properties.name: Ad Navalia
properties.notes: Ad Navalia sat on the Ligurian coast road at modern Varazze, its name meaning "at the shipyards." The station marked a Roman naval building yard on this stretch of coast, part of the string of small ports and stopping points the Via Julia Augusta strung together between Genua and Vada Sabatia.

properties.name: Alba Docilia
properties.notes: Alba Docilia stood at modern Albisola Superiore, named for the Ligurian tribe of the Docilii. Excavators found its remains near the town's railway station in the late 1800s, a 2nd-century way-stop on the cursus publicus between Genua and Vada Sabatia.

properties.name: Vada Sabatia
properties.notes: Vada Sabatia, at modern Vado Ligure next to Savona, marked the point where the coast road met the inland route to Aquae Statiellae. The Antonine Itinerary places it 33 Roman miles from Genua, making it a major junction on the Ligurian coast.

properties.name: Pullopice
properties.notes: Pullopice was a mansio the Antonine Itinerary places 12 miles past Vada Sabatia, on the stretch of coast now split between Borgio Verezzi and Finale Ligure. No excavation has fixed its exact find-spot, so its location is a best estimate rather than a confirmed dig.

properties.name: Albingaunum
properties.notes: Albingaunum, modern Albenga, was chief town of the Ligurian Ingauni and still shows a Roman amphitheater among its standing remains. The Via Julia Augusta left the town through the Porta d'Arroscia, and a stretch of its original paving survives on the road toward Alassio.

properties.name: Lucus Bormani
properties.notes: Lucus Bormani, at modern Diano Marina, took its name from Bormanus, a Ligurian god of sacred springs. Travelers broke their journey here between Capo Berta and Capo Cervo, a wooded refreshment stop rather than a walled town.

properties.name: Costa Balenae
properties.notes: Costa Balenae was a coastal landing station at the mouth of the Argentina river, excavated today as the Capo Don archaeological area near Riva Ligure. Both the Antonine Itinerary and the Peutinger Table record it on the run toward Albintimilium.

properties.name: Albintimilium
properties.notes: Albintimilium, modern Ventimiglia, was the chief town of the Intemelii and the last major Italian station before the road climbed into the Maritime Alps. Its Roman theater still stands, along with the excavated street grid of a working municipium.
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre of Albintimilium, Ventimiglia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman theatre at Ventimiglia, ancient Albintimilium

properties.name: Lumone
properties.notes: Lumone, now Roquebrune-Cap-Martin's Carnolès quarter, was a mansio administered from Albintimilium. Its 1st-century funerary mausoleum, three vaulted arches carrying traces of frescoed plaster, still stands beside the old road and gave the station its name.

properties.name: Alpe Summa (Tropaeum Alpium)
properties.notes: Alpe Summa, at modern La Turbie, marked the point the Antonine Itinerary itself calls where Italy ends and Gaul begins. Augustus raised the great Tropaeum Alpium here in 6 BCE to commemorate his conquest of the Alpine tribes, and its ruined tower still crowns the pass over Monaco.

properties.name: Cemenelum
properties.notes: Cemenelum, now the Cimiez district of Nice, was capital of the small province of Alpes Maritimae, deliberately sited above the older Greek port of Nikaia rather than through it. Its amphitheater and bath complex still stand among the best-preserved Roman remains on the French coast.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre of Cemenelum, Cimiez district of Nice · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman amphitheatre (arènes de Cimiez) at Cemenelum, Nice

properties.name: Ad Varum
properties.notes: Ad Varum marked the crossing of the Varus river, the boundary the Itinerary tracks between Cemenelum and Antipolis. It was a ford rather than a town, and the river's mouth has since shifted, so its pin sits at the crossing's approximate historical location near modern Saint-Laurent-du-Var.

properties.name: Antipolis
properties.notes: Antipolis, today's Antibes, began as a Greek colony of Massilia before becoming a Roman town on the coast road. Sections of its ancient ramparts still stand, alongside a small museum built into a later fort on the original Roman site.

properties.name: Ad Horrea
properties.notes: Ad Horrea, "at the granaries," stood at modern Mandelieu-La Napoule. Excavators found extensive grain-storage remains matching the Itinerary's distance readings from both Antipolis and Forum Iulii, confirming a supply depot on the coast road.

properties.name: Forum Iulii
properties.notes: Forum Iulii, modern Fréjus, was Augustus's own naval colony, home port to part of the fleet that had fought at Actium. Its amphitheater, aqueduct and harbor works still rank among the best-preserved Roman military infrastructure on the French coast.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Iter a Vintimilio Arelate usque)
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre of Forum Iulii, Fréjus · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman amphitheatre at Fréjus, ancient Forum Iulii

properties.name: Forum Voconii
properties.notes: Forum Voconii was a roadside vicus occupied from roughly 50 BCE into the early 3rd century CE, now identified near the Les Blais hamlet by Le Cannet-des-Maures. Its location was disputed among several nearby villages for decades before excavation finally pinned it down.

properties.name: Matavonium
properties.notes: Matavonium, at modern Cabasse in the Var, is confirmed by Roman milestones and inscriptions found on site. It sat on the coast road midway between Forum Voconii and Ad Turrem.

properties.name: Ad Turrem
properties.notes: Ad Turrem, modern Tourves in the Var, is fixed by Roman milestones recovered along the old road bed. It was the last stop before the road climbed toward Tegulata and the approach to Aquae Sextiae.

properties.name: Tegulata
properties.notes: Tegulata is placed by the Antonine Itinerary and the Peutinger Table between Ad Turrem and Aquae Sextiae, with Pourrières and neighboring Puyloubier both proposed as its find-spot. No excavation has settled which of the two candidate villages is correct.

properties.name: Aquae Sextiae
properties.notes: Aquae Sextiae, today's Aix-en-Provence, was the oldest Roman settlement in Gaul, founded in 122 BCE by the consul Sextius Calvinus around its thermal springs. Marius crushed the Teutones outside its walls in 102 BCE, a battle still remembered on the road two centuries later.
properties.image_credit: Roman sarcophagus from Aquae Sextiae · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ancient Roman sarcophagus excavated at Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence)

properties.name: Massilia
properties.notes: Massilia, modern Marseille, was the great Phocaean Greek colony that kept its own civic identity as an allied city under Rome rather than becoming a colonia. The coastal Itinerary route from Vintimilium to Arelate runs directly through it, not around it.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Iter a Vintimilio Arelate usque)
properties.image_credit: Musée des Docks Romains, Marseille (ancient Massilia) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Calcaria
properties.notes: Calcaria, "the lime-works," was a quarrying and lime-burning station on the road skirting the north shore of the Etang de Berre between Massilia and Arelate. Vitrolles and Les Pennes-Mirabeau are the two competing candidates for its exact site, neither confirmed by excavation.

properties.name: Fossae Marianae
properties.notes: Fossae Marianae, modern Fos-sur-Mer, grew up around the canal Marius's troops cut in 102 BCE to link the Rhone to the sea, later worked commercially by Massilia and then Arelate. It served as one of Arelate's outports at the delta's edge.

properties.name: Arelate
properties.notes: Arelate, modern Arles, is the named endpoint of the Antonine Itinerary's coastal route from Vintimilium. Caesar settled it with veterans in 46 BCE, and its amphitheater, theater and forum were all long complete by Trajan's reign.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Iter a Vintimilio Arelate usque)
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre of Arelate, Arles · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Roman amphitheatre at Arles, ancient Arelate

properties.name: Glanum
properties.notes: Glanum, just south of modern Saint-Remy-de-Provence, sat on the stretch of road linking Cabellio to Arelate. Its mausoleum and arch, known locally as Les Antiques, still stand together beside the site, among the best-preserved Roman monuments anywhere in Provence. The road continued east from here to the Rhone crossing at Ernaginum before reaching Arelate.
sources: Itin. Ant. (A Mediolano Arelate per Alpes Cottias)
properties.image_credit: Mausoleum of the Julii at Glanum, Les Antiques, near Saint-Rémy-de-Provence · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Roman mausoleum of the Julii still standing at Glanum

properties.name: Ad Fines
properties.notes: Ad Fines, "at the boundary," marked a territorial edge on the road between Apta Julia and Cabellio, its name a common Roman label for a station sitting on a border between civic territories.
sources: Itin. Ant. (A Mediolano Arelate per Alpes Cottias)
