properties.name: Pertusa
properties.notes: Pertusa stood 14 Roman miles from Carthage on the road to Hippo Regius, the first stage travelers reached leaving the provincial capital. The town grew into a Christian bishopric answering to Carthage. Its remains are identified with El-Haouaria, now a western suburb of Tunis.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Iter a Carthagine Hippone Regio)

properties.name: Unuca
properties.notes: Unuca appears in the Antonine Itinerary as a stop 7 Roman miles beyond Pertusa on the road to Hippo Regius. No ruin or inscription has ever been matched to the name — its plotted position here comes from the itinerary's mileage alone, interpolated between its better-documented neighbors.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Iter a Carthagine Hippone Regio)

properties.name: Sicilibba
properties.notes: Sicilibba sat 13 Roman miles from Unuca on the road to Hippo Regius and held its own bishopric under the Church of Carthage. Later scholarship tentatively places its ruins at Alaouine in the Tunisian interior, but the site has never been excavated to confirm it.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Iter a Carthagine Hippone Regio)

properties.name: Membressa
properties.notes: Membressa stood 17 Roman miles from Sicilibba on the road to Hippo Regius, at a crossing of the Bagradas river. The town lasted into the Byzantine period and gave its name to a 536 CE battle fought there. Its site is occupied today by the Tunisian town of Medjez el-Bab.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Iter a Carthagine Hippone Regio)

properties.name: Musti
properties.notes: Musti stood 35 Roman miles from Membressa on the road to Hippo Regius and already held municipium status under Augustus. Under Trajan the town built a temple to the Cereres and travelers crossed the Bagradas there on a stone bridge. Its forum and temples still stand at the site of El Krib.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Iter a Carthagine Hippone Regio)

properties.name: Naraggara
properties.notes: Naraggara stood 32 Roman miles from Sicca Veneria at the junction where the road to Hippo Regius split from the inland road to Cirta. Livy placed the final battle of the Second Punic War, fought between Scipio Africanus and Hannibal in 202 BCE, in its immediate vicinity. The site is identified with modern Sakiet Sidi Youssef on the Tunisian-Algerian border.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Iter a Carthagine Hippone Regio; the Iter a Musti Cirtam gives the adjoining Sicca-Naraggara leg as 30 mp, a manuscript variant)

properties.name: Thagaste
properties.notes: Thagaste lay 25 Roman miles from Naraggara and 53 miles short of Hippo Regius on the inland road through Numidia. The Berber-Roman town later became famous as the birthplace of Augustine of Hippo in 354 CE. Its ancient remains lie largely unexcavated beneath the modern Algerian city of Souk Ahras.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Iter a Carthagine Hippone Regio)

properties.name: Thagora
properties.notes: Thagora branched off 20 Roman miles from Naraggara on the road running inland from Musti to Cirta. Originally a Carthaginian trading post, it minted its own bronze coinage before becoming a Roman civitas. Its ruins near Taoura, Algeria include a bath complex and a later fortress.

properties.name: Tipasa in Numidia
properties.notes: Tipasa in Numidia lay 24 Roman miles from Thagora on the road from Musti to Cirta, in the Numidian highlands. Not to be confused with the better-known coastal Tipasa in Mauretania, its Punic name meant a stopover or place of passage, a role the station kept under Rome. Its fortress walls still stand near modern Tiffech.

properties.name: Gasaufula
properties.notes: Gasaufula stood 35 Roman miles from Tipasa on the road from Musti to Cirta and is identified with the Roman town of Gadiaufala. The settlement grew into a bishopric under the Metropolitan of Cirta. Its remains lie at Ksar Sbahi in Algeria's Oum El Bouaghi Province.

properties.name: Sigus
properties.notes: Sigus stood 33 Roman miles from Gasaufula and 25 miles short of Cirta on the final stretch of the road from Musti. The town's surviving Latin inscriptions document a busy Roman civic life. Its site is occupied today by the Algerian commune of the same name in Oum El Bouaghi Province.

properties.name: Bordeaux
properties.notes: Burdigala anchored the western end of the Via Aquitania on the Garonne, shipping wine and pottery out through a harbor busy enough to draw the notice of the poet Ausonius. The road left the city gate and struck south across the Landes toward the Pyrenean foothills and, eventually, the Mediterranean. Its amphitheater held roughly 15,000 spectators. The Palais Gallien ruins still stand where its arena once did.
properties.image_credit: Palais Gallien, the Roman amphitheatre of Burdigala, Bordeaux · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruined arches of the Palais Gallien, the Roman amphitheatre of ancient Burdigala in Bordeaux

properties.name: Bazas
properties.notes: Vasatas served the Vasates tribe as their civitas capital and gave its name to the whole surrounding Bazadais district. Travelers leaving Burdigala changed horses at two relay posts before reaching this walled town on its limestone spur above the Beuve valley. Its cathedral square now covers the old Roman core.

properties.name: Eauze
properties.notes: Elusa grew into the wealthiest town of Novempopulana and later its provincial capital, a status its Roman walls and townhouses still reflect. Workmen digging a cellar in 1985 turned up the Eauze treasure, a hoard of 28,000 silver coins and gold jewelry buried around 261 CE. The finds now fill a purpose-built museum on the site of a Roman house.
properties.image_credit: Musée archéologique du Trésor d'Eauze · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The archaeological museum at Eauze, built on the site of Elusa's Roman houses and home to the Eauze treasure of 28,000 coins

properties.name: Auch
properties.notes: Ausci, capital of the Auscii, sat on a hill over the Gers river where the pilgrim road from Burdigala bent east toward Tolosa. The Antonine geographer Ptolemy and the Bordeaux pilgrim both marked it as a full civitas stop rather than a mere relay. Roman foundations still turn up under the old town's stepped stairways.

properties.name: Marsan
properties.notes: Ad Sextum took its name from its position six leagues out of Ausci, a plain distance-marker rather than a proper town. The Bordeaux pilgrim's 333 CE itinerary logged it as a routine horse-change on the long haul toward Tolosa. Archaeologists have narrowed its footprint to the streams south of modern Marsan without pinning an exact building.

properties.name: Gimont
properties.notes: Hungunuerro broke the road partway between Ausci and Tolosa, one of the relay names the Bordeaux pilgrim recorded without further comment in 333 CE. Local antiquarians place it at Gimont, on the Gimone river the modern bastide town still straddles. No standing Roman masonry has been confirmed at the exact spot.

properties.name: L'Isle-Jourdain
properties.notes: Bucconis stood seven leagues from Ausci at a spot called La Gravette south of what is now L'Isle-Jourdain. Excavations there turned up the relay's foundations and confirmed a working horse-change on the Tolosa road since the early Roman conquest. The Bordeaux pilgrim recorded it by name on his 333 CE march east.

properties.name: Leguevin
properties.notes: Ad Iovem, named for a wayside shrine to Jupiter, was the last change of horses before travelers reached Tolosa. Local tradition and the sequence of leagues in the Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary set it at modern Leguevin, a short ride out of the city. No temple foundation has surfaced to confirm the dedication behind the name.

properties.name: Toulouse
properties.notes: Tolosa was the great hinge of the Via Aquitania, a Volcae Tectosages stronghold the Romans turned into the largest city in Gaul after Narbo lost ground. Its temple treasury was famous enough that a Roman general's plundering of it in 106 BCE spawned the proverbial phrase aurum Tolosanum, ill-gotten gold. From here the road ran on toward Narbo and the sea.

properties.name: Baziege
properties.notes: Badera was the first stop east of Tolosa, fixed at 15 Roman miles by both the Peutinger Table and a milestone still kept inside the parish church of Saint-Etienne. First-century wine-amphora debris found near its cemetery points to a busy trade in imported Italian wine. The settlement sat where the road crossed the Hers river.

properties.name: Col de Naurouze
properties.notes: Elusio sat at the low pass of Naurouze, the watershed ridge where roads and later canals switched between draining to the Atlantic and to the Mediterranean. Cicero mentioned the place in a courtroom speech of 69 BCE, decades before Rome paved the road past it. By the time the Peutinger Table was drawn the stop had already faded from the map.

properties.name: Castelnaudary
properties.notes: Sostomagus marked the 38th Roman milestone out of Tolosa on the road east to Narbo, a Gaulish market name meaning roughly clean or pure market. The Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary of 333 CE logged it as a routine change station on the day's ride toward Carcaso. Modern Castelnaudary grew over the same crossing on the Fresquel river.

properties.name: Bram
properties.notes: Eburomagus, its Gaulish name meaning yew-tree market, grew into the busiest roadside settlement between Tolosa and Narbo. Excavations along the old road bed have traced its street grid running straight out from the town's western gate. Medieval Bram later rebuilt itself as a near-perfect circle of houses ringing the same ancient site.

properties.name: Carcassonne
properties.notes: Carcaso held a fortified hilltop above the Aude river where the Via Aquitania crossed paths with the north-south route into the mountains. Roman-era wall footings still underlie stretches of the medieval Cite's inner defenses, reused stone upon reused stone. The name itself survived every rebuilding to reach the modern city unchanged.

properties.name: Lezignan-Corbieres
properties.notes: Hosuerbas was the last change of horses before Narbo, set down by the Bordeaux pilgrim some 15 Roman miles short of that city. Later surveys of the road bed place its footprint near the hamlet of Gaujac by modern Lezignan-Corbieres. Nothing of the relay stands above ground today.
